title: F1 bosses agree V8 engines deal from 2030
text:
Formula 1 bosses are close to a deal that will see V8 turbo hybrid engines replace the current controversial engines in 2030.

McLaren chief executive officer Zak Brown said an "agreement in principle" had been reached by engine manufacturers and F1 bosses on the new rules.

These will be for a 2.1-litre V8 turbo engine with a smaller electrical element than this year, as first revealed by BBC Sport last month.

Some details remain to be resolved but the main core of the rules has been agreed.

The electrical element will be for a maximum power output of 200kW - compared with 350kW this year.

But only half of that will be available at all times, with the remaining half used only for an overtake mode.

A key element of the rules will be to remove the issue of energy starvation that has been criticised by the drivers this year for taking away "pure" racing.

But the overall power output of the engines will be similar to now.

The combustion engine will have about 780bhp, while 200kW is 270bhp.

That means a total power output of 1,050bhp in overtake mode or just over 900bhp in standard running.

Brown said: "Everyone is very, very excited. Now it's about kind of dotting the i's and crossing the t's.

"I'm excited for the new engines, I think everyone will be, the power units. But there's a lot more also going on to continue to evolve the sport. So, between the FIA and Formula 1, they're doing a great job."

Russell fastest in Las Vegas practice after rain

How to follow Las Vegas Grand Prix on the BBC

Alpine executive director Flavio Briatore said: "We have the agreement, basically. It's not signed, but it looks like everybody's agreed to 2030 V8s, and I'm very happy.

"It's the right way to go. We need an engine with a lot of noise, and a simple engine, and we need to be racing with that."

The ruleset amounts to a compromise reached by manufacturers after FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially pushed for a naturally aspirated engine without turbo or electrical components.

But these were required to reduce overall fuel consumption, and therefore weight at the start of races.

That means Ben Sulayem's desire for a return to the loud volumes of the previous V8 era from 2006 to 2013 will not be achieved. The engines are expected to sound similar to now.

This was important because a significant increase in engine noise would have put at threat some races in city centres that are commercially important to F1, such as Miami and Las Vegas.

The 2.1-litre capacity has been arrived at because it amounts to adding to two cylinders to the current 1.6-litre V6 blocks, with the aim of reducing development costs.

Cars are expected to start races with about 110-120kg of fuel, up from about 100kg now. A total weight limit of 150kg for the power-units will be imposed, down by about 30kg from the current engines.

There will be a fuel energy flow limit to keep the power of the combustion engine under control, and a budget cap figure for engines set at $190m (£145m) per year.

As part of negotiations, General Motors, backers of the Cadillac team, will delay the production of its new engine until 2030. It had been scheduled for 2029.

In return, GM will lose its voting rights on current engine rules and be classified as a new manufacturer from 2030.

The team will continue to use Ferrari customer engines through 2029.

Cadillac F1 chief executive officer Dan Towriss said: "For a period of time, we were working on both. So, they've already got a V6 base to build off of, and working towards the V8.

"There are a number of designs that are in motion now, and so there's a lot of good foundation for what we're trying to build and the direction we're headed in."

title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
text:
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.

Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.

It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.

"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.

Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.

"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.

Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.

"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.

"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.

Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.

But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?

In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.

But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".

But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.

"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.

Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".

While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.

She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.

"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination."

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement.

Evangeline Atkinson had a frustrating experience over her credit score.

"I was at university, paying rent, paying bills, as I had been doing for many years. I tried to get a £30-a-month phone contract, and they said no," she recalls.

"When I dug into it, it was because I was completely invisible to the system. No record could be found for me at any of the big three credit reference agencies."

That experience inspired her to try to change the system.

In 2021, Atkinson founded a credit reference agency with her best-friend from school, who had also experienced difficulties getting credit.

Their firm, Noggin HQ, was authorised by the FCA in June. Atkinson explains it was set up to help consumers access affordable credit by analysing their current account transactional data.

The platform helps lenders interpret thousands of individual data points about a person's spending habits.

Crucially, it does this without using AI, which Atkinson has also argued "carries the risk of inbuilt bias".

"You have to be very careful", she warns. "It's very sensitive data and it would be very easy for the models to be inferring various kind of protected characteristics."

Perhaps conscious of change, the big three credit scoring firms have all started experimenting with AI.

Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August 2026, letting users check their credit score inside ChatGPT. Equifax launched a platform called Equifax Amplify AI, which it says uses machine learning to sharpen credit assessment and fraud detection.

Meanwhile, in March TransUnion announced it was integrating Google's Gemini models "within its proprietary analytic data assets".…

title: The art of protection - inside an F1 helmet factory
text:
As soft, instrumental opera music plays in the background of a precise temperature-controlled room in northern Italy, Thomaso is using a children's toy ball and hairdryer to perform his meticulous work.

Hugely focused, in a crisp white coat, he moulds a precious sticky black material over and over again for up to six hours.

One day, his fastidiousness may save the life of one of the best athletes in the world.

The room Thomaso works in is called "the magic shop". Its motto? 'One man, one shell.'

Much of what happens inside is top secret. What we can say is the black material Thomaso is working with is a blend of carbon fibre that has to be stored at exactly -16°C. He moulds it into a secret form, layer by layer, after which the entire unit is baked in a vacuum bag at a set pressure at 120C for three-and-a-half hours.

The handmade products he is working on are personally chosen by their clients - for their safety features, as well as comfort, practicality and look.

Thomaso's colleague Sven travels the world between February and December to keep those clients happy. A different country almost every week, with a reliable weather forecast almost as important as a large allowance of hand luggage.

Together with 32 colleagues, Thomaso and Sven work for one of the four leading manufacturers of F1 helmets.

They produce sophisticated engineering masterpieces, and works of art.

"Our philosophy is to make the best product for the best drivers," says chief executive Alberto Dall'Oglio.

In the early days of grand prix racing, protection was rudimentary. Drivers often wore little more than leather flying caps, goggles and - eventually - relatively basic open-face helmets.

Safety standards were inconsistent, materials primitive and the consequences of an accident frequently devastating.

According to the official F1 website, Giuseppe Farina - the first winner of an F1 race and first world champion - competed wearing nothing more than "his trusty cloth cap, two pairs of goggles (he wore the spare pair round his neck), cotton dungarees, leather boots and leather gloves".

The arrival of the full-face helmet in the late 1960s marked a defining moment. Bell introduced its pioneering Star model in 1966, and Dan Gurney became the first driver to race in a full-face helmet in 1968. The face - previously exposed to flying debris, fire and impact - finally had meaningful protection.

Progress was painfully slow, and motorsport's darkest moments repeatedly exposed the limitations of the technology.

In 1976, Niki Lauda 's Ferrari erupted into flames at the Nurburgring. His helmet came loose, leaving his head exposed to the fire. He survived, but suffered severe burns and lifelong injuries. The accident became a defining lesson in the importance of helmet retention, fire resistance and the protection of the driver's entire head.

The tragic deaths of Roland Ratzenberger and Ayrton Senna at Imola in 1994, followed by Jules Bianchi's fatal accident at Suzuka in 2014, demonstrated even increasingly sophisticated helmets could not eliminate every danger.

Ratzenberger suffered a fatal basilar skull fracture; Senna succumbed to multiple fractures of the skull base, after a strut from the suspension pierced his helmet.

Bianchi's accident exposed the vulnerability of drivers' heads to heavy external impacts. Helmets are only one part of a much wider safety system, which now includes stronger survival cells, the Hans device and the halo.

In 2004, the FIA introduced its new helmet safety standard, requiring advanced carbon-fibre construction to deliver greater strength, improved impact protection and reduced weight for F1 drivers.

At Bahrain's Sakhir circuit in 2020, Romain Grosjean's Haas split apart against the barriers and burst into flames. After 28 seconds trapped in the wreckage, he emerged with burns to his hands and ankles. His Bell helmet, fire-resistant equipment and the halo were instrumental in saving his life - a powerful testament to decades of safety innovation and engineering.

"Today's helmets are withstanding up to 30 seconds at 700, even 800, degrees," says Dall'Oglio. "Then they have to self-extinguish within 15 seconds."

Dall'Oglio is the CEO of Schuberth Performance, Thomaso an engineer and Sven a racing service technician, working trackside at more than 400 grands prix, preparing helmets and visors for rain, sun or floodlights.

Needing to avoid any impact on the helmets, he must carry them - sometimes five or six at a time - to races.

Schuberth, a German firm, has a long history in head protection. Founded in 1922, the company began making industrial products before moving into helmet linings in the late 1920s, then mining and motorcycle helmets in the 1950s.

With its HQ in Magdeburg and F1 helmet production in Schio, northern Italy, it produces special helmets for military forces - made of Kevlar, and some of a similar carbon - in the same factory as the F1 helmets.

Its motorsport credentials grew considerably around the turn of the millennium.

Following Michael Schumacher's British Grand Prix accident in 1999, Schuberth developed a new generation of racing helmets, subsequently worn by Schumacher and other leading drivers.

Of the current drivers, four-time world champion Max Verstappen is the most prominent to wear a Schuberth helmet. He is joined by Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar, Cadillac's Sergio Perez, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Arvid Lindblad at Racing Bulls.

Dall'Oglio's team hand-makes about 250 helmets a year.

An F1 helmet is a remarkable marriage of science and aesthetics.

Constructed using advanced composite materials, including carbon fibre, it must be exceptionally strong while remaining light enough to minimise strain on a driver's neck.

Visors, ventilation systems, fire-resistant linings, communication equipment, a straw-like drinks system and carefully designed retention mechanisms all contribute to its performance.…
